questions.question: How do economies of scale and diseconomies of scale affect the long-run average cost curve in traditional analysis? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• How do economies of scale and diseconomies of scale affect the long-run average
  • cost curve in traditional analysis?
  • Economies of Scale (Falling Segment): As output expands in the long run, a firm experiences
  • real and financial economies of scale (e.g., labour specialisation, technical efficiencies, bulk
  • purchasing discounts). This leads to a decline in per-unit cost of production, causing the Long-
  • Run Average Cost (LAC) curve to slope downward.
  • Constant Returns to Scale: At an optimum scale of production, the firm experiences constant
  • returns to scale, where increasing output does not change the average cost. At this point, the
  • LRAC reaches its minimum.
  • Diseconomies of Scale (Rising Segment): Beyond the optimal scale of production (Minimum
  • Efficient Scale), further expansion results in managerial inefficiencies, coordination failures, and
  • communication bottlenecks. Per-unit costs begin to rise, causing the LAC curve to slope upward.
  • Net Effect: The interplay between economies and diseconomies of scale gives the traditional
  • LAC curve its characteristic U-shape.

questions.question: Explain why long-run equilibrium in a perfectly competitive market eliminates both supernormal profit and loss. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In the long run, a perfectly competitive market eliminates both supernormal
  • profits and losses due to the mechanisms of free entry and exit of firms in the
  • industry. When existing firms earn supernormal profits, new firms are attracted to
  • enter the market. This increases the total supply of the good, leading to a decrease in
  • market price. Entry continues until all firms are only making normal profits, where
  • price equals average cost, and supernormal profits are no longer possible.
  • If firms are incurring losse s in the short run, some will eventually exit the industry.
  • As firms leave, the supply decreases, causing the market price to rise. Exit continues
  • until the remaining firms are also only making normal profits —where price once
  • again equals average cost, and further losses are eliminated

• Illustrate the second-degree price discrimination with real-life examples.
  • Second-degree price discrimination occurs when a seller charges different per-unit prices for
  • different quantities or blocks of the same product or service, without individual customer
  • profiling. The firm sets a price schedule (block pricing/quantity discounts) where the price per
  • unit decreases as the quantity consumed increases, capturing a portion of consumer surplus.
  • Real-Life Examples:
  • Utility Tariffs (Electricity/Water): Lower rate per unit for the first 100 kWh, and different tiered
  • rates for subsequent blocks of usage.
  • Bulk Purchases: "Buy 2, Get 1 Free" or wholesale discount pricing (e.g., per single unit vs. per
  • unit if bought in packs of 10).
  • Data Plans / Telecom Services: Tiered broadband plans based on data volume consumed.

  • continues to fall. SATC reaches its minimum at the absolute full capacity point. It has a broad

questions.question: Bring out the differences between monopoly and monopsony. / [CO3]
questions.solution_html:
• In a monopoly, one firm supplies a particular good or service and can set prices
  • without competition from other sellers. This seller has market power, usually
  • resulting in higher prices and fewer choices for consumers. Monopolies are regulated
  • by antitrust laws to prevent abuse of power and promote competition.
  • In a monopsony, one buyer dominates the market for a good or service, controlling
  • its demand. The buyer can influence prices, often resulting in lower prices or wages
  • for sellers or workers. Monopsonies often lead to market inefficiencies, such as
  • lower wages in labor markets.

questions.question: Describe Revealed Preference theory. / [CO1] [6x5 = 30]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe Revealed Preference theory.
  • Introduced by Paul Samuelson (1938) to explain consumer demand behavior empirically without
  • using subjective notions like utility or indifference curves. Consumer preferences are "revealed"
  • through observed choices in the market under given budget constraints.
  • Key Axioms:
  • • Strong Ordering: The consumer selects a unique bundle of goods out of all affordable
  • bundles available within their budget constraint.
  • • Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP): If bundle is chosen over bundle when both
  • are affordable ( is revealed preferred to ), then can never be chosen over at any other price-
  • income situation where is also affordable.
  • Samuelson derived the Law of Demand directly from WARP using basic consistency
  • assumptions, proving that a negative income effect is not required to establish a downward-
  • sloping demand curve for normal goods. Revealed preference theory states that the consumer's
  • product or service choice under different income and price levels provides information about
  • Page 15 of 2
  • their preferences. For example, if there were two combinations of goods (A and B) and if the
  • consumer chooses A (which is expensive) over B, then the consumer reveals their preference for
  • A over B. The theory is based on the premise that consumers are rational thinkers who compare
  • many options before making a decision. As a result, when a consumer selects one choice over
  • another, it must be the one they prefer. When a consumer's consumption pattern is determined by
  • observing the bundle of goods they choose over other alternatives, when all of them are within
  • the budget is known as revealed preference. A budget line is a diagram that depicts the
  • combination of products that a consumer can purchase at a certain income and price level. If
  • bundle a is revealed preferred over bundle b in budget set B, then the WARP says that bundle b
  • cannot be revealed preferred over bundle a in any budget set B'. This would be equally true had b
  • been located anywhere else on or below the blue line. The bundle c will not violate WARP even
  • if it is chosen in budget set B', because it is not on or below the blue line of affordable choices at
  • the time of the observed choice of a.
